name: Carpal tunnel syndrome
aliases: median nerve compression at the wrist
median neuropathy at the carpal tunnel

reference.source: Apley & Solomon's System of Orthopaedics and Fractures
clinicalPearls: The commonest peripheral nerve entrapment, caused by compression of the median nerve beneath the flexor retinaculum at the wrist
Typically presents with numbness, tingling, and pain in the thumb, index, middle, and radial half of the ring finger, characteristically worse at night and relieved by shaking the hand
Symptoms may radiate up the forearm; in advanced cases there is weakness and wasting of the thenar muscles (abductor pollicis brevis)
Often idiopathic but associated with pregnancy, diabetes, hypothyroidism, rheumatoid arthritis, obesity, and repetitive wrist use
Provocative signs include Tinel's (tapping over the nerve) and Phalen's (sustained wrist flexion) tests, though their sensitivity is limited
Nerve conduction studies confirm the diagnosis and grade severity, and are useful before surgery or in atypical cases
Mild or intermittent disease often responds to nocturnal wrist splinting, activity modification, and treatment of any underlying condition; corticosteroid injection can give temporary relief
Surgical division of the flexor retinaculum (carpal tunnel release) is indicated for persistent symptoms, failure of conservative treatment, or established motor deficit and sensory loss
reference.pathophysiology: The carpal tunnel is a rigid osseofibrous canal bounded by the carpal bones and roofed by the flexor retinaculum, through which the median nerve passes alongside the flexor tendons. Any increase in the contents or reduction in the capacity of this fixed space raises pressure on the median nerve. Compression impairs the nerve's microcirculation and, if sustained, causes segmental demyelination and eventually axonal loss. Conditions that increase tissue volume (fluid retention in pregnancy, synovial thickening in rheumatoid arthritis, tenosynovitis from overuse) or reduce tunnel size (wrist fractures, deformity) precipitate symptoms. Sensory fibres are usually affected first, with motor weakness and thenar wasting appearing later.
additionalDifferentials: Proximal median nerve entrapment (e.g. pronator syndrome)
additionalInvestigations: Nerve conduction studies and electromyography to confirm and grade median nerve compression
Clinical provocative tests (Tinel's and Phalen's) and thenar strength assessment
Blood tests for associated conditions (glucose/HbA1c, thyroid function) where indicated
Wrist radiographs if there is a history of fracture, deformity, or arthritis
Ultrasound of the nerve in selected or atypical cases
redFlags: Progressive thenar muscle wasting and weakness indicating advanced nerve damage warranting timely decompression
Persistent dense sensory loss that may not fully recover
Acute severe symptoms after a wrist fracture suggesting acute median nerve compression
Bilateral or rapidly progressive neuropathy suggesting a systemic cause needing investigation
reference.prognosis: Most patients with mild to moderate disease improve with conservative measures or gain lasting relief from surgical release; however, longstanding severe compression with thenar wasting and marked axonal loss may leave incomplete recovery of strength and sensation despite decompression.
pitfalls: Attributing hand symptoms to carpal tunnel syndrome when the cause is cervical radiculopathy or a more proximal lesion
Delaying surgery until irreversible thenar wasting and sensory loss develop
Overlooking a treatable underlying condition such as hypothyroidism or diabetes
Relying solely on provocative clinical tests, which can be falsely negative
references: Apley & Solomon's System of Orthopaedics and Fractures
